title: Control-Flow Defects, Unreachable Code and Loop Termination
learningObjectives: Identify common control-flow defects such as missing branches, accidental fall-through and incorrect loop conditions.
Explain how unreachable statements differ from code that is merely unlikely to execute.
Use loop invariants and progress measures to reason about termination.
Recognize how break, continue, return and error paths affect cleanup and program state.
Test control flow with branch coverage, boundary cases and explicit expected outcomes.

understand.concept: Control flow describes the order in which statements execute. Defects arise when branches are incomplete, conditions are incorrect, loop state fails to progress, or a control-transfer statement skips required work. Unreachable code cannot be executed along the program's control-flow paths, while code that is difficult to reach may still be reachable. Termination reasoning asks whether every intended execution eventually reaches an exit under stated assumptions.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding Common control-flow errors, unreachable code and termination reasoning (CodeSaathi extension) helps you reason about program behaviour instead of memorizing syntax. It is useful in exams, debugging and building reliable C applications.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a tool with a precise contract: it has valid inputs, defined operations and observable results.
understand.analogyLimit: An analogy is only an aid; the C standard and the relevant function specifications determine actual behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Common decision defects

An if/else chain can omit an important case, order overlapping conditions incorrectly, or contain an else attached to a different if than intended. Use braces and test every branch, including invalid input.

## 2. Unreachable versus unlikely code

A statement after an unconditional return in the same block is unreachable. By contrast, a branch guarded by a rare condition may be reachable even if ordinary tests never take it. Do not label code unreachable merely because it was not observed during one test.

## 3. Loop termination

For each loop, identify its invariant, termination condition and progress measure. A progress measure should move toward a state that makes the condition false. Check whether arithmetic overflow, input failure or a skipped update can prevent progress.

## 4. Control transfers and cleanup

break exits the nearest loop or switch; continue advances the current loop; return exits the function. Before using these statements, identify which updates, file closes, memory releases or other cleanup actions might be skipped. Structure cleanup paths deliberately.

## 5. Testing control flow

Create tests for every branch, loop zero/one/many iterations, boundary values, early exits and failure paths. Assertions and branch coverage can help reveal missing cases, but tests do not prove all paths correct. Review the control-flow logic and its assumptions.

examples.title: A loop with a clear progress measure
examples.explanation: The progress measure is remaining. Each iteration decreases it by one, so the condition eventually becomes false for the initial value shown.

examples.title: Avoid skipping required progress
examples.explanation: The continue branch updates index before skipping the rest of the iteration. Without that update, the loop would repeatedly encounter index == 2 and never progress.

practise.guidedTask: Draw a simple control-flow trace for a loop with normal completion, an early break and an input-failure path. Mark every update and cleanup operation, then verify each path against the code.
practise.independentTask: Review a short program containing nested if statements and a loop. Identify unreachable statements, missing branches, possible non-termination and skipped cleanup. Rewrite only the defective control flow and add tests for each identified path.
hints: Distinguish unreachable code from code that tests have not yet reached.
Identify the state that changes on every loop iteration.
Trace every break, continue and return to its target.
Check that all resource cleanup paths are handled.
Test boundary and failure paths as well as the normal path.

questions.prompt: What is a useful way to reason about loop termination?
options: Identify a progress measure that moves toward making the condition false
Assume every loop runs a fixed number of times
questions.answer: Identify a progress measure that moves toward making the condition false
questions.explanation: A progress measure helps show why a loop eventually terminates under stated assumptions.

options: A statement after an unconditional return in the same block
A branch guarded by a rare condition
questions.answer: A statement after an unconditional return in the same block
questions.explanation: Execution has already left the function before reaching that statement.

questions.prompt: Why can continue cause an infinite loop?
options: It may skip an update required to make the loop condition false
It resets every variable to zero
questions.answer: It may skip an update required to make the loop condition false
questions.explanation: The skipped update may be the loop's only progress step.

questions.prompt: What should be checked when adding an early return?
options: Whether required cleanup and state updates still occur on that path
Whether the function name is uppercase
questions.answer: Whether required cleanup and state updates still occur on that path
questions.explanation: Early exits can bypass resource release or other required work.

questions.prompt: What does branch coverage help reveal?
options: Branches that tests have not executed
Every possible input for every program
questions.answer: Branches that tests have not executed
questions.explanation: Coverage identifies untested branches but does not prove correctness.
